items.prompt: Sort the materials into soluble and insoluble in water.
hints: A soluble material seems to disappear when you stir it into water.
An insoluble material can still be seen, or it settles at the bottom.
Think about stirring sugar into tea, then stirring sand into water.
items.explanation: Sugar, salt and instant coffee dissolve in water, so they are soluble. Sand, chalk, flour, iron filings and marbles do not dissolve, so they are insoluble.

items.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: the liquid that does the dissolving
the mixture made when a solid dissolves
hints: In salty water, the salt is one part and the water is another part.
Solution is the name for the whole mixture, not for one part of it.
Start with the word insoluble. The letters in- at the start often mean not.
items.explanation: In salty water, salt is the solute, water is the solvent and the salty water is the solution. A material that does not dissolve is insoluble.

items.prompt: Mira stirs sugar into warm water. The sugar seems to disappear. What has happened to it?

options.text: It has melted.
options.why: Melting needs heat to turn one solid into a liquid on its own. Sugar in water dissolves.

options.text: It has gone forever.
options.why: The sugar is still there. You can taste it, and you can get it back by evaporating the water.

options.text: It has broken into pieces too small to see, spread through the water.
It has turned into water.
options.why: The sugar does not change into water. It mixes with the water.

hints: If the water tastes sweet, the sugar must still be in it somewhere.
Think about the difference between melting and dissolving.
Cross out the choices that say the sugar is gone or has changed into something else.
items.explanation: The sugar has dissolved. It has broken up into particles too small to see, which spread out through the water, so the water tastes sweet.

items.prompt: Choose 2 ways to make sugar dissolve faster.

options.text: stir the water
use warmer water
use bigger lumps of sugar
options.why: Bigger lumps dissolve more slowly. Smaller grains dissolve faster.

options.text: use colder water
options.why: Sugar dissolves more slowly in cold water.

options.text: put a lid on the glass
options.why: A lid does not change how fast sugar dissolves.

hints: Think about how you make sugar dissolve in a cup of tea quickly.
Moving the water and heating the water both help the sugar to mix in.
Cross out the choices that would slow dissolving down or make no difference.
items.explanation: Stirring and using warmer water both make sugar dissolve faster. Crushing the sugar into smaller grains would help too.

items.prompt: Dewi dissolves 20 g of salt in 200 g of water. What is the mass of the salt solution?
hints: When salt dissolves, it is still there, even though you cannot see it.
Nothing is lost when a solid dissolves, so the masses add together.
Start by adding the mass of the water to the mass of the salt.
items.explanation: Dissolving does not destroy the salt, so its mass is still there. 200 g + 20 g = 220 g of salt solution.

solution.say: The salt dissolves, but it does not disappear. Its mass is still in the glass.
Add the mass of the water and the mass of the salt.

items.prompt: Ahmad times how long a spoonful of sugar takes to dissolve in water at different temperatures. What does the bar chart show?

figure.alt: Bar chart of time for sugar to dissolve: 120 seconds at 20 °C, 75 seconds at 40 °C, 45 seconds at 60 °C and 25 seconds at 80 °C.

options.text: The hotter the water, the slower the sugar dissolves.
options.why: The bars get shorter as the water gets hotter, so dissolving takes less time.

options.text: Sugar does not dissolve in cold water.
options.why: At 20 °C the sugar still dissolved. It just took longer.

options.text: Temperature makes no difference.
options.why: The times are very different at each temperature.

options.text: The hotter the water, the faster the sugar dissolves.

hints: Each bar shows the time taken. A shorter bar means a shorter time.
Compare the bar for the coldest water with the bar for the hottest water.
Read the time at 20 °C and at 80 °C. Decide which is quicker.
items.explanation: The time to dissolve falls from 120 seconds at 20 °C to 25 seconds at 80 °C. So the hotter the water, the faster the sugar dissolves.

items.prompt: Which of these is dissolving, not melting?

options.text: butter turning to liquid in a hot pan
options.why: Heat turns the butter from a solid into a liquid on its own. That is melting.

options.text: coffee granules mixing into hot water
ice turning to water in the sun
options.why: That is melting. Only one material is involved.

options.text: chocolate going soft in your hand
options.why: Warmth from your hand melts the chocolate.

hints: Melting needs only one material and heat. Dissolving needs a solid and a liquid.
For each choice, count how many different materials are involved.
Look for the choice where a solid mixes into a different liquid.
items.explanation: Coffee granules dissolve when they mix into the water and spread through it. Butter, ice and chocolate melt because heat turns each one from a solid into a liquid on its own.

items.prompt: Arif keeps adding salt to a glass of water and stirring. Soon, salt stays at the bottom however long he stirs. Why?

options.text: The water cannot dissolve any more salt, so the solution is saturated.
The salt has turned into sand.
options.why: The salt is still salt. It stops dissolving because the water cannot hold any more.

options.text: Stirring has made the salt insoluble.
options.why: Stirring helps salt dissolve faster. It does not stop it dissolving.

options.text: All the water has evaporated.
options.why: The water is still in the glass. It simply cannot hold any more salt at this temperature.

hints: There is a limit to how much salt one glass of water can dissolve.
Think about what happens when you keep adding sugar to a small cup of tea.
Cross out the choices that say the salt or the water has changed into something else.
items.explanation: A glass of water can only dissolve a certain amount of salt. When no more will dissolve, the solution is saturated, and any extra salt stays at the bottom.

items.prompt: Ana says that sugar melts in tea. Is she right? Explain the difference between melting and dissolving, with an example of each.

criteria.label: Says that sugar dissolves in tea
Explains dissolving: a solid spreads through a liquid
Explains melting: heat turns one solid into a liquid
Gives a correct example of each

planning: What happens to sugar in tea?
What happens to ice in the sun?
How many materials are involved each time?
items.model: Ana is wrong, because sugar dissolves in tea. Dissolving happens when a solid breaks into tiny pieces that spread through a liquid, like salt in water. Melting happens when heat turns a solid into a liquid on its own, like ice turning into water in the sun.
hints: Think about whether the sugar needs the tea, or only heat, to change.
Melting needs heat and one material. Dissolving needs a solid and a liquid.
items.explanation: Sugar dissolves in tea because it spreads through the liquid as tiny pieces. Melting is a change from solid to liquid caused by heat, with only one material involved.

items.prompt: At 20 °C, 100 g of water can dissolve about 36 g of salt. How much salt can 250 g of water dissolve at 20 °C?
hints: The more water there is, the more salt it can dissolve.
250 g of water is two and a half lots of 100 g.
Find the salt for 200 g of water first, then the salt for the extra 50 g.
items.explanation: 250 g of water is 2.5 times 100 g, so it can dissolve 2.5 × 36 g = 90 g of salt. Any salt beyond this would stay undissolved.

solution.say: 100 g of water dissolves 36 g of salt, so 200 g of water dissolves twice as much.
50 g of water is half of 100 g, so it dissolves half of 36 g.
